items.desc: Manuscript of the Yemenite-Baladi rite, with the commentary of ʻEts ḥayim by Yaḥyā Ṣaliḥ, possibly written as a [scribal] master copy, likely preceding the printing of the Yemenite Tiklāl with this commentary in Jerusalem, 1894. Written in a Yemenite-Sephardic semicursive script (commentary), with some portions written in a Yemenite square script (such as the Psalms for the eve of Purim, f.26r-34r); the Baladi rite was practiced mostly in the Ṣanʻāʼ environs in Yemen.
items.extent: 1 item (ii, 198, iii leaves) : paper ; 14 x 11 cm

items.collection: Penn Digital Collections
items.title: Middle Eastern pressed flowers album, between 1876 and 1888
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Penn Digital Collections
items.place: Middle East -- Description and travel
items.desc: This volume contains pressed flowers from cities across the Middle East region including Antioch, Bethlehem, Damascus, Jerusalem, Mount Carmel, Mount Lebanon, Nazareth, Sidon, and Tyre. On each page, there is an arrangement of dried flowers (sometimes in a shape, such as a cross, a star and crescent or an anchor), and text in English and Arabic. In English, the text generally identifies a location or the type of the flower and a Bible reference. Identified flowers/plants include almond, "bitter herb," cedar needles, daisies, ferns, fig leaves, grasses, henna, immortelles (curry), Kharub (carob), lentiles, mustard, olive leaves, pulse, reeds, rose of sharon, saffron, and thorns. On occasion, when a page is titled, "flowers of ...", there is a mix of unidentified flowers arranged together. This is the case for Bethlehem, the Antioch, Tyre, and Jerusalem. The volume has olive wood covers and is lacking a spine.

items.title: Cohn Bros., Clifton, Miss. account book, 1878-1879
items.creator: Cohn Bros
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Mississippi
items.desc: A leather volume comprising the daily credit and debit accounts of Cohn Bros. in Clifton, Mississippi spanning over one year from April 1, 1878 to December 31, 1879.  The account book documents the transactions of Cohn Bros.  Included are entries of purchases of various dry goods and sundries.  Customer names are often listed along with their purchases.  Some items sold and purchased included bacon, burlap, candles, coffee, cotton, flour, fabric, freight, pork, postage stamps, seeds, sugar, thread, tobacco, and whiskey.  Written on first page: Cohn Bros. Clifton, Miss. April 1st, 1878.  Stamps on first page read: Cohn Bros. Clifton near Rodney, Miss.  Page numbers are pre-printed 2-320.  Pages 70-100 and pages 250-320 are blank.

items.title: Glen Park Hotel register, 1878-1883
items.creator: Glen Park Hotel (Watkins Glen, N.Y.); Frost, Charles Sherwood, 1835-1906; Frost, George W., 1864-1902
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: New York (State) -- Watkins Glen
items.type: manuscripts (documents); codices (bound manuscripts); registers (lists); visitors' books; notebooks; blank forms; forms (documents)
items.desc: An oversize volume with pre-printed pages comprising the register for the Glen Park Hotel in Watkins Glen, New York.  The register spans the years from 1878 to 1883.  Guests staying at the hotel included many Jewish families.  Each year a musical ensemble or band would stay at the hotel such as the Wellsville Cornet Band in 1878 and the Germania Band in 1881.  The Foster School of Clifton Springs, N.Y. also stayed at the hotel a few summers.  Guests arrived at Glen Park Hotel from across the United States including states surrounding New York, the Midwest, and from as far as California, Colorado, Louisiana, and Texas.  Guests also traveled from Canada, Europe, and South America.  Each page in the volume is pre-printed with the heading: Glen Park Hotel, Watkins, N.Y., C. S. Frost, prop'r.  Columns with headings room, time, name, residence, and remarks were printed on each page.  Some handwritten remarks appear in pencil throughout the register to indicate extra costs for boats, carriages, horses, telegrams, trunks, and wash.  The signature of George W. Frost, son of Charles S. Frost, appears on the inside covers and in the volume.  One guest's name has been excised from the volume on July 1, 1880.  Several pages in the volume are detached and some are torn at the bottom edge.

items.title: Crayon enlargement portrait of Kauffman Strauss
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A period crayon enlargement portrait of Kaufman Strauss, whose commercial and domestic life in 1880 San Francisco is documented in nineteenth-century city directories and Achenbach Foundation archives. Kaufman managed a successful hauling and logistics enterprise at 3 Battery Street supported by family members as foreman and bookkeeper, anchoring his household within the vibrant Gilded Age German-Jewish community near local synagogues and commercial markets.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: Crayon enlargement portrait of Sarah Strauss
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A period crayon enlargement portrait documenting Sarah Frank Strauss alongside her husband Kaufman Strauss, whose footprint in Gilded Age San Francisco is preserved through 1879–1880 city directories and archival records from the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Kaufman operated a prominent hauling and teaming business out of Battery Street within the city's bustling mercantile district, and the family resided on Tyler Street (now Golden Gate Avenue), reflecting the structured domestic and religious life of the city's German-Jewish community.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: Hand-colored photograph portrait of Dora Getz
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A hand-colored photographic portrait of Dora Getz, depicting a prominent German-Jewish pioneer who left a lasting legacy in California through business savvy, community service, and civic leadership. Beginning their journey in Lower Lake, Lake County, California, in the late 1870s and 1880s where Solomon established a general merchant supply business, the family later relocated to San Francisco around 1889. There, Solomon and Dora became veteran real estate developers over a 35-year career, platting major tracts in the Richmond and Sunset Districts and accumulating substantial success. Deeply woven into the cultural and religious fabric of the San Francisco Jewish community, their philanthropic activities secured their place as representative figures of early Western Jewry.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: Hand-colored photograph portrait of Solomon Getz
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A hand-colored photographic portrait of Solomon Getz, a prominent German-Jewish pioneer and real estate developer in California. Following early mercantile success supplying mining and agricultural workers in Lower Lake, Lake County, Solomon and Dora relocated to San Francisco around 1889. Solomon transitioned entirely into real estate, developing major tracts in expanding neighborhoods such as the Richmond and Sunset Districts and amassing a significant fortune. Active in both commercial and civic spheres—including serving as Senior Deacon for the Clear Lake Masonic Lodge—Solomon and Dora remained pillars of San Francisco's early Jewish pioneer community until their passing.

items.title: Moroccan piyut book ; manuscript; פיוט כתב-יד נוסח מרוקו
items.creator: Amar, D. A.
collections: Elis & Ruth Douer Endowed Fund
items.place: Morocco -- Casablanca; Morocco -- Casablanca
items.desc: This is a manuscript of collected Hebrew poetry, or piyutim, from the Moroccan tradition of piyut. Many of the poems are written by David ʻAmar (a 19th century Moroccan paytan), as evidenced by his name appearing in acrostic forms (such as the poem ʻIdan duḥḳah, which has a bold title of Daṿid [ʻAmar] ḥazaḳ, f. 95v-96r); likely, the manuscript was written over a period of time. It appears as if the manuscript was meant as a source of Moroccan and even Casablanca piyut; other authors mentioned include Masʻud (or Massoud) ḥazaḳ, who wrote Piyuṭ ha-RaSh.b.I. (after Shimon bar Yoḥai, f. 94v-95r); Yaʻaḳov ha-levi, writing a poem in honor of R. Yitsḥaḳ Nahon (f. 56v-7v; he lived in Tetouan, Morocco, in the 19th century); a poem in honor of R. ʻAmram ibn Dayan (and naming him as the same as Amram ben Diwan, a cabalist and emissary for the settlement in Jerusalem (Jerusalem 1740 - Ouazzane 1782, f. 151r-151v); and a piyut by "Shelomoh" for the coming of the Messiah (f. 178r-178v). Written in a Moroccan cursive script with headings and highlighted words in square script; the bulk of the manuscript was written in ink (f. 1r-179r) and the end written in pencil (f. 179v-194v). The folios are commercial lined paper and are yellowed and brittle; the volume is bound in boards with a deteriorating brown-leather spine, likely original. Written in Morocco, likely in Casablanca. There is a table of contents in the beginning (f. 1r-4r) and at the end (f. 182r-194v).; Manuscript of collected Hebrew poetry, or piyutim, from the Moroccan tradition of piyut. items.title: Portrait Charcoal / Drawing of Gustav Gump
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A large-scale charcoal portrait of Gustave Gump executed around 1880 by renowned California artist Giuseppe Cadenasso and commissioned by the Pioneer Art Company. Gustave Gump was a prominent German-born Jewish pioneer, merchant, and art connoisseur who co-founded S. & G. Gump: Mirrors, Mouldings, and Paintings, establishing San Francisco's first commercial fine-art gallery around 1880. As an elite tastemaker catering to post-Gold Rush millionaires, Gump balanced his commercial empire with active involvement in Congregation Emanu-El. This historic portrait was formerly preserved in the permanent collections of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco before entering the Kaplan Collection.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: Portrait Crayon drawing of Aaron Cahn
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A crayon enlargement portrait of Aaron Cahn, a foundational Jewish pioneer, merchant, and communal leader. After establishing early roots in Omaha, Nebraska (co-founding M. Hellman & Company), Cahn returned to the Pacific Coast, building significant commercial and property interests in San Francisco. He served as an early director of Congregation Emanu-El, sat on the executive building committee for its landmark Sutter Street Synagogue, and dedicated over four decades of service as Vice-President of the Eureka Benevolent Association, directing charitable relief and immigrant integration.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: Portrait Crayon drawing of Babette Weil
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A crayon photographic enlargement portrait commemorating Babette Weilheimer (born Babette Strauss in Baden, Germany). Alongside her husband Samuel Weilheimer—a foundational Peninsula merchant who established early general stores in Mountain View—Babette anchored her family in the civic and religious sphere of San Francisco's Congregation Emanu-El.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: Portrait Crayon drawing of Marcus Getz
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A hand-finished crayon enlargement portrait of Marcus Getz, highlighting his status among San Francisco's 19th-century merchant-class elite. Alongside his brother Joseph and wife Etta, Marcus transitioned from frontier general store operations in Lower Lake, California, into the international wholesale and agricultural export powerhouse Getz Bros. & Co. Active within elite Jewish fraternal circles such as B'nai B'rith and the Concordia-Argonaut Club, Marcus and Etta maintained deep communal ties to Temple Emanu-El and local philanthropic institutions.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: Portrait Crayon drawing of Samuel Appel
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A period crayon enlargement portrait of Samuel Appel, a prominent Gold Rush-era Jewish pioneer, decorated San Francisco Fire Department member, and participant in the Committee of Vigilance. Appel engaged in early commercial ventures, including the historic Appel & Dietrich Market on California Street, and helped establish early Jewish communal and cultural foundations in the city. Members of his pioneering family circle are interred at the historic Hills of Eternity Memorial Park in Colma, California.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: Portrait Crayon drawing of Yetta Getz
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A hand-finished crayon enlargement portrait capturing Etta (Yetta) Cohen Getz, a prominent figure in 19th-century San Francisco Jewish society. Arriving from Prussia during the post-Gold Rush era, Marcus and Etta established foundational mercantile enterprises that evolved into the international trading empire Getz Bros. & Co. Etta was deeply engaged in women's auxiliary networks, organizing social welfare programs for newly arriving immigrants and supporting organizations like the Eureka Benevolent Society alongside her multi-generational affiliation with Temple Emanu-El.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: Private ledger / R. Sidenberg, 1880-1891.
items.creator: Sidenberg, Richard 1846-1932.
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: United States -- New York -- New York; United States -- New York
items.desc: A leather bound volume comprising the personal accounts of Richard Sidenberg spanning the years from 1880 to 1891. Preceding the 311 numbered pages is tabbed alphabetical index. The index consists chiefly of company names. The ledger records Sidenberg's accounts, banking transactions, bonds, deposits, and dividends. The ledger is divided into several sections indicated by a heading at the top of each page. The sections include cash account, inventory account, income or profit and loss account, properties by addresses, individual railroad accounts, banks, and insurance companies. Toward the end of the volume are recorded monthly profits and expenses of the G. Sidenberg Co. There are small accounts regarding individuals of the Sidenberg family including his wife and children. There are several notations and items crossed out in the volume. Title is stamped in gold on cover. A metal, locking closure is attached to the covers. Pages 304-311 are blank.

items.title: Sharḥ ʻal ha-Torah, 1880?-1930?; שרח על התורה, 1880-1930
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Penn Digital Collections
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: This is a manuscript of a commentary in Judeo-Arabic explaining the Pentateuch. It is incomplete; it is missing the first three parshiyot and begins in parashat Ṿa-yera, and finishes at the beginning of parashat Haʼazinu. It is written in long lines on commercial lined paper with the vertical bounding lines ruled in lead. It is written with a cursive Eastern script similar to contemporary Syrian Hebrew manuscripts. In the margins, there are notes indicating where the portions of the Parashah are in the text. The folios are very brittle. Bound in contemporary boards with yellowed endpapers, likely original.
items.extent: 193 leaves : paper ; 190 x 140 (170 x 110) mm bound to 200 x 140 mm

items.creator: Jacobson, Rosa, 1868-1956
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Pennsylvania -- Philadelphia
items.type: manuscripts (documents); codices (bound manuscripts); autograph albums; Autograph verse; Manuscripts, American
items.desc: A red, leather, oblong volume with decorative, stamped covers entitled Autographs.  The volume contains autographs of friends and relatives spanning the years from 1881 to 1907.  A majority of the signatures range in date from 1881 to 1883.  Poetic sentiments, well wishes, and some drawings addressed to Rosa precede each signature.  Autographs from the year 1883 were chiefly from her confirmation classmates.  One autograph signed by a cousin Constance Jacobson is dated 1907. Some autographs are written in German.  A color-printed, decorative title page reads: Paragon autograph album.  Spine is lacking, front cover is detached, and some leaves are loose.

items.desc: Pasted on cover: Hexagon-shaped sheet of paper with a concentric hexagonal motif rendered in blue lines that diminish in thickness toward the outer edges. At the center appears the handwritten title Synagogen Gesänge, along with a provenance note identifying Rabbi Nussbaum as owner in 1881. The manuscript is possibly written by more than one hand, as suggested by variations in script.; Written in blue and black inks, with the number of staves varying throughout.; Texts are in romanized Hebrew; titles appear primarily in Hebrew script, with a few in Latin script; additional text is in German written in Latin script.; "26.6.92." items.creator: Bannānī, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, 1720 or 1721-1780; Qaṣṣārah, ʻAlī ibn Idrīs, -1843 or 1844; Gannūn, Muḥammad al-Tihāmī
collections: Fez Lithographs Collection (University of Pennsylvania)

items.desc: Title from colophon.; Commentary and supercommentary on al-Sullam al-murawniq (or al-murawnaq) by ʻAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad al-Akhḍarī, itself a versification of Athīr al-Dīn al-Abharī's Arabic adaptation of Porphyry's Isagoge.; Lithographed.; Commentary in the margins. Includes catch words. Text is in Maghribi script, and is partially pointed and vocalized.; Pages numbered: 1-240, 233-236.; "Ammā baʻd fa-hādhihi taqāyīd tatashawwafu li-ʻarāʼis khudūrihā al-adhhān wa-taqādīr tatasharrafu bi-samāʻ mabānīhā al-ādhān mawḍūʻah ʻalá sharḥ al-Sullam lil-imām al-rabbānī al-ḥāʼiz qaṣab al-sabq fī istikhrāj farāʼid al-fawāʼid min baḥr al-maʻānī Abī ʻAbd Allāh Sayyidī Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan Bannānī ..."--P. 2.; "... Qad tamma ṭabʻ sharḥ al-ʻālim al-ʻallāmah al-muḥaqqiq al-fahhāmah al-mudaqqiq Abī ʻAbd Allāh Sayyidī Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Bannānī ... ʻalá al-Sullam al-murawniq fī ʻilm al-manṭiq maʻa ḥāshiyatihi lil-ʻallāmah al-darrākah al-fahhāmah Abī al-Ḥasan Sayyidī ʻAlī ibn Idrīs ibn ʻAlī Qaṣṣārah"--P. 236 [i.e. 244].; "Bi-taṣḥīḥ muṣaḥḥiḥihi ʻalá ḥasab ṭāqatihi wa-wusʻihi wukkila min mubayyaḍat muʼallifihi ʻadá al-malzamah al-ūlá min al-sharḥ wa-al-thalāthah al-uwal min ḥāshiyatihi ʻabīd rabbihi wa-asyar dhanabihi Muḥammad al-Tuhāmī ibn al-Madanī Gannūn kāna Allāh la-hu fīmā kāna wa-yakūnu ʻalá dhimmat al-shābb al-anmaq al-muʻallim al-Sayyid al-ʻArabī al-Azraq"--P. 236 [i.e. 244].; "Sammaytuhu bi-al-Sullam al-murawniq yurqá bi-hi samāʼ ʻilm al-manṭiq ..."--P. 31.; Acquired for the Penn Libraries with assistance from the Allan G. Chester and Florence K. Chester Fund.; Handlist #16.; Penn Libraries' copy in original binding (type 2). Text block is detached from binding.; Original binding (type 2). Text block is detached from binding.

items.title: Hādhā al-taʼlīf al-sharīf al-musammá bi-al-Tasliyah wa-al-sulwān, li-man ibtalá bi-al-idhāyah wa-al-buhtān ..; هذا التأليف الشريف المسمى بالتسلية والسلوان، لمن ابتلى بالاذاية والبهتان ..
items.creator: Ibn al-Madanī Jannūn, Muḥammad, -1884 or 1885
collections: Fez Lithographs Collection (University of Pennsylvania)
Allan G. Chester and Florence K. Chester Fund
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: Lithographed.; Margins have miscellaneous sermons and letters by the author; "Ḥamdan li-man fataqa ratq samāʼ anwār masāʼil ʻulūm al-sharīʻah, wa-rabaṭa bi-hā azmat al-ẓawāhir wa-al-bawāṭin ṭardan lil-ʻaks wa-manʻan lil-shabah wa-saddan lil-dharīʻah, ḥattá imtāza al-shaqī wa-al-saʻīd wa-al-mukrih wa-al-ṭāʼiʻ, wa-tabayyana al-qāʼim wa-al-rākiʻ wa-al-sājid wa-al-rātiʻ, fa-al-saʻīd man waṣala bi-ḥablihā fa-tamassaka bi-al-ʻurwah lā [?] al-wuthqá, wa-al-shaqī man ḥāha [?] ʻan ṭarīqihā wa-āthara al-ḥayāh al-dunyā wa-al-ākhirah khayr wa-abqá, wa-al-ṣalāh wa-al-salām ʻalá sayyidinā wa-mawlānā Muḥammad ʻayn al-raḥmah al-ʻāmmah lil-ʻāmmah wa-al-khāṣṣah, wa-shams al-hidāyah al-mushrifah min aflāk qulūb khāṣṣat al-khāṣṣah, al-baḥr alladhī tadaffaqat minhu amwāj sharāʼiʻ jamīʻ al-anbiyāʼ wa-al-mursalīn, ṣalawāt Allāh wa-salāmuhu ʻalayhim ajmaʻīn.  Hādhā wa-inna hādhā al-taʼlīf al-sharīf al-musammá bi-al-Tasliyah wa-al-sulwān, li-man ibtalá bi-al-idhāyah wa-al-buhtān, shāmil min al-sharīʻah bi-ḥaddihi jamīʻ afrād al-ḥusn, jāmiʻ min al-balāghah fī ʻaqd lafẓihi wa-maʻnāhu bayna jawhar al-hāmish wa-durr al-matn muraṣṣaʻ bi-yawāqīt al-maʻqūl wa-al-manqūl munaẓẓam bi-zabarjad al-ḥikmah wa-dībāj al-faḍl al-mawhūb wa-al-masʼūl, bi-shaykhinā al-imām aʻlam al-aʻlām dhawī al-albāb wa-al-afhām, al-ʻulamāʼ al-ʻāmilīn al-rāsikhīn ʻalá qadam khayr al-anām, man taṣaddá li-nuṣrat dīn al-ḥaqq al-mafrūḍ wa-al-masnūn, li-yuḥiqqa al-ḥaqq wa-yubṭila al-bāṭil wa-li-dhikrihi al-mujrimūn al-ḥabr al-baḥr al-niḥrīr al-darrākah al-naffāʻah khātimat al-muḥaqqiqīn shaykh al-jamāʻah Sīdī Muḥammad ibn al-Madanī Gannūn adāma Allāh baqāʼahu, wa-abbada fī al-saʻādah irtiqāʼahu, amīn amīn, wa-al-ḥamd lillāh rabb al-ʻālamīn"--Full t.p.; Pages are divided into 20 (quarto) sections, plus 3 pages of a 21st section.  Each page bears number 1-8.; Collated.  Includes catch words.  Text is in Maghribi script, and is partially pointed and vocalized.; Acquired for the Penn Libraries with assistance from the Allan G. Chester and Florence K. Chester Fund.; Handlist #18.; Penn Libraries' copy in original binding (type 2). Partially detached.; Penn Libraries' copy has lengthy handwritten note on flyleaf.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: Congregation B'nai Israel minute book, 1885-1906
items.creator: Congregation B'nai Israel (Keokuk, Iowa)
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Iowa -- Keokuk
items.desc: This oversize volume is comprised of minutes from meetings of officers and the board and trustees of Congregation B'nai Israel in Keokuk, Iowa spanning the years from 1885 to 1906.  The written records of the meetings are in chronological order and signed by the current secretary of the congregation.  The meetings discussed all aspects of the congregation and the synagogue.  Regular, special, trustee, and yearly meetings were chiefly held at the synagogue and occasionally at homes and businesses of members.  Meetings were held by the officers of the B'nai Israel.  Recorded are discussions concerning advertising, books, building maintenance and rental, burial plots, choir,  the cemetery, committees, deaths, donations, dues, finances, fund raising, Hebrew school, High Holiday planning, membership, rabbis' contracts, resignations, and taxes.  Searching for a rabbi to serve the congregation was ongoing during this time period.  No quorum was noted when meetings were canceled.  Several Jewish families active in the community and as officers of the congregation are noted throughout the volume such as the Carwalho, Hirsch, Lowitz, Lyons, Spiesberger, Stern, and Vogel families.  Several mentions of the Women's Society activities and donations are written throughout the minutes. The last two leaves comprise a handwritten copy of the 1855 deed for the cemetery dated 1902.  Stamp on first leaf: Lowry News Dealer, booksellers & stationers Keokuk, Iowa.  The pages are ruled and have stamped numbers 1-384.  Pages 209-383 are blank.

Hādhā sharḥ Kitāb Kasr al-shahwatayn shahwat al-baṭar wa-shahwat al-faraj wa-huwa al-kitāb al-thālith min Kitāb al-Iḥyāʼ -- Title embedded in text on p. 220. Hādhā sharḥ Kitāb Āfat al-lisān wa-huwa al-kitāb al-rābiʻ min al-rubʻ al-thālith al-mawsūm bi-al-muhlikāt min Kitāb al-Iḥyāʼ -- Title embedded in text on p. [344]. Hādhā sharḥ Kitāb Dhamm al-ghaḍab wa-al-ḥiqd wa-al-ḥasad wa-huwa al-khāmis min al-rubʻ al-thālith min Kitāb al-Iḥyāʼ ....; Acquired for the Penn Libraries with assistance from the Allan G. items.title: [A collection of Russian, Ukrainian, and other popular folk and other types of dances, Including Jewish Traditions]
items.creator: Peĭsakhovich, Zepl; Fraystut, Seni︠a︡ Peĭsakhovich, compiler; Skornyĭ, O. B.; Shteĭnberg, M. K.
collections: Gratz-Mandell Jewish Music Collection (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.lang: Multiple languages; French; Italian; Russian; Ukrainian
items.type: manuscripts (documents); Waltzes (Music); Mazurkas (Music); Quadrilles (Music); scores (documents for music); Manuscripts; Dance music
items.desc: Some of the titles listed in the contents note may not accurately correspond to the works included in this compilation. This is because the source material appears to be quite old and in fragile condition, with handwriting that is extremely faint and written in highly individualized styles. These factors make it difficult to interpret the original titles with certainty, and some readings may be approximate.; Title devised by cataloger.; Titles and textual elements occur in multiple languages--principally Russian, Ukrainian, Italian, and French--inscribed in both Cyrillic and Latin scripts; numerous entries are faint, irregular, or otherwise difficult to decipher.; Unnumbered pagea 116 conatins a table of contents presented in Cyrillic script, and the facing page appears to contain a handwritten primer or reference guide on musical notation.; On unnumbered page 114, the lower portion of the manuscript page functions not as musical repertoire but as pedagogical material. It contains a two-octave pitch sequence--likely a C-major scalar framework--extending across both treble and bass clefs, suggesting practice with the full grand staff. The dense use of ledger lines indicates deliberate training in reading and notating extreme registers. Below this, repeated treble-clef symbols and evenly spaced whole-note heads resemble handwriting and spatial-placement exercises. A large ornamental flourish at the center aligns with common 19th-century scribal habits. Collectively, the notation reflects foundational skill development rather than compositional intent, consistent with a student's workbook or a teacher's demonstration page.; Related Work: Cherniavsky, Joseph, 1895-1959. Pesn'.
items.extent: 1 ms. score (192 unnumbered pages of notated music, 2  blank pages)

items.title: Broadside for the Central Republican Club featuring Horace Davis
items.creator: Lilienthal, R. I.
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A rare 1890 political broadside printed in bold blue text on cream-colored paper by C. A. Murdock & Co. for the Central Republican Club, presided over by Horace Davis. The poster lists selected delegates for upcoming Republican state, congressional, and city conventions, notably highlighting prominent local Jewish political figures such as Alferd Castle and G. W. Dinkelspiel for state/congressional conventions, and R. L. Lilienthal for the city convention. The piece provides significant documentation of early San Francisco political history and Gilded Age civic participation.

items.desc: Lithographed.; Collated. Includes catch words. Text is in Maghribi script, and is partially pointed and vocalized.; Pages are divided into 4 quires, plus 7 pages of a 5th quire.  Each page bears a number 1-8.; "Hādhā al-Khatm al-mubārak lil-faqīh al-ʻallāmah al-muḥaqqiq al-mushārik Abī ʻAbd Allāh Sayyidī al-Ḥājj Maḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʻAbd al-Salām Jannūn allafahu ḥīna khatama Mukhtaṣar al-Imām Sayyidī Khalīl bi-Jāmiʻ al-Qarawīyīn aṭāla baqāʼahu Allāh wa-adāma al-nafʻ bi-hi amīn"--Full t.p.; Collection handlist, and bibliography (al-Maṭbūʻāt al-ḥajarīyah fī al-Maghrib) indicate that this book was published in Ṣafar 1310 A.H. [August-September 1892].; "Qad khatama Mukhtaṣar Sayyidī Khalīl ... yawm al-Aḥad al-muwāfiq li-Thāmin ʻashar shahr Ṣafar al-khayr sanat Thalāthimiʼah wa-ʻAsharah wa-Alf ..."--P. [34].; Includes laudatory poems by ʻAbd al-Raḥmān al-ʻIrāqī and Ibrāhīm al-ʻAlawī.; Acquired for the Penn Libraries with assistance from the Allan G. Chester and Florence K. Chester Fund.; Handlist #28.; Penn Libraries' copy:  binding is cardboard (type 3).  Pages of 5th quire [p. 33-39] are unbound.

items.title: Presentation Walking Cane — Charles Wessolowsky (1890)
items.creator: Wessolowsky
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Early American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: A gold-filled repoussé handle presentation walking stick cane inscribed, "Presented to Chas Wessolowsky by the Jewish Youngmen of Albany, Ga. 1890." Charles Wessolowsky was a key figure in Albany history, a Civil War veteran of the 32nd Georgia Infantry, a Grand Master Mason, a state legislator, and associate editor of the Jewish South newspaper. He was a foundational leader in establishing regional Jewish institutions, including Albany's Hebrew Benevolent Society and religious school, and his letters were compiled in Reflections of Southern Jewry.

items.collection: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Modern American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.title: K. Straus and Company Inc. account book, 1893-1894.
items.creator: The company was founded by Karl Straus born in 1845 who was a Jewish German immigrant. Straus arrived in Philadelphia in 1867 and he began a wholesale liquor business. In 1888 he became a tobacco merchant opening his own company named K. Straus & Co. Straus died in 1920 leaving the business to his nephew Adolf Loeb who incorporated the company in 1922.; K. Straus and Company Inc.
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Modern American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: United States -- Pennsylvania -- Philadelphia; United States -- Pennsylvania
items.desc: A slim, pre-printed volume comprising the daily purchases and sales of tobacco by Philadelphia tobacco merchant K. Straus & Co. spanning a little of over one year from 1893 to February 1894. Accounts were recorded on the pre-printed pages spanning one opening. Leaf tobacco purchased was entered on the rectos and leaf tobacco sold was entered on the versos. A printed heading across top of the two-leaf opening reads: Record of leaf tobacco purchased and sold by followed by blank lines. Written In the blank spaces is K. Straus & Co. at 122 N. 3rd St. Phila. The company purchased tobacco from various merchants from around the United States and Havana, Cuba. K. Straus & Co. tobacco sales served chiefly patrons of Pennsylvania, Delaware, and New Jersey area with occasional sales to customers in Charlottesville, Virginia.

items.type: manuscripts (documents); ketubahs; marriage certificates; blank forms
items.desc: Printed ketubah form with manuscript ketubah text in black ink in Aramaic and Hebrew in Rabbinic semi-cursive script. Stylized, colored border frames three sections: a narrow rectangle at top with words of blessing in Aramaic in square script; a middle section with two arches filled with ketubah text and supported by three columns; and a larger rectangle at bottom with words of blessing in Hebrew in square script. Numerous layers of patriarchy listed for both groom and bride who trace their ancestry to the exiles of the Spanish Inquisition. Wedding took place on 23 Siṿan 5657 (23 June 1897), in Tangier, Morocco. Groom also signed. Some loss of text along fold lines.
items.extent: 1 leaf : paper, color illustrations ; 67.7 X 46.4 cm

items.desc: From the important financier and philanthropist Jacob Schiff to the noted American Jewish jurist and communal leader Mayer Sulzberger. Thanks him for sending the circular draft "to be issued by the Bible Committee...it proves a carefully thought out document." Schiff returns it to the judge with alterations suggesting that it be "...printed in pamphlet form and accompanied by a circular [discussing] the financial part." Discusses names for the committee and whether to add the names of the rabbis who contribute translations.

items.title: Meʼir Schön poetry book, 1900?-1914; מאיר שאֶן ספר-שירים, 1900?-1914
items.creator: Schön, Meʼir
collections: Penn Digital Collections
items.place: Slovakia -- Košice; Slovakia
items.type: manuscripts (documents); codices (bound manuscripts); poems; manuscripts for publication; black-and-white photographs; Meditations
items.desc: This is a manuscript book of poetry by Meʼir Schön, likely a rendering of his archive of poems into a manuscript for publication. Introduction (f. 2r-13v) details the author's exhaustive toil of lifelong Hebrew study (he admired the contributions to the study of Hebrew of Naphtali Hirz Wessely, Joseph Kohen-Zedek, Avrom Ber Gotlober, Solomon Rubin, Isaac Baer Levinsohn, Max Emanuel Stern, among others (f. 7r; additionally quoting Mordecai b. Abraham Banet on f. 8r)). Poems include a memorial for his parents and teacher (f. 15r-16v), poems for holidays, meditations on old age and death, a long poem of homebuilding as a parable for life's toil (f. 59r-99r); a section called Shirat dodim contains poems written for friends and relatives (such as a poem for a friend on his fiftieth anniversary in the rabbinate; f. 115v); the names of the subjects are replaced by an ellipsis. An afterword indicates that the manuscript was completed on the eve of Rosh ha-Shanah 5674 (September 20, 1914). Written mostly in stanzas on commercial lined paper (binder holes in gutter), rebound in buckram; written in an Ashkenazic cursive script, with highlights in a square script; select words and accents vocalized.
items.extent: 1 item (239 leaves) : paper ; 220 x 143 mm + 1 photograph

items.desc: Miscellany written for Yaʻaḳov ben Mordekhai Gabbai containing ʻEṭ sofer, a work with document formularies for use in a Bet din (financial, social, and philanthropical documentation); novellae, possibly written by Gabbai; and Goralot (a method of predictive speculation using Zodiac and Hebrew names; attributed to Abraham ibn Ezra in this manuscript (f. 17r)). items.title: Zidduk ha-din : Liturgical use of Portugal-Lisbon ; manuscript; צדוק הדין : מנהג ליסבון
items.creator: Querub, Moses
collections: Penn Digital Collections
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: Lisbon Sephardic liturgy surrounding the deathbed, funeral, and mourning cycle, adopted and confirmed by the established community (title page (f. 2r); the new community, formed during the final decades of the 19th century, mostly composed of Jews from Morocco and Gibraltar, and the Synagogue Shaaré Tikvah consecrated in 1904); the liturgy follows the Viduy (confession), funeral, Zidduk ha-din (f. 3r-4v), and the liturgy around the preparation of the dead for funeral (f. 5r-20r). Written in Sephardic square and semicursive scripts (most of the text), with some written in Solitreo cursive (such as f. 20v-21r), in the hand of former owner Moses Querub (his inscriptions preceding and following the manuscript; recording the death of his father, Shem Tov bar David Querub, on f. 1r, and his additional inscription dated September 1908, Lisbon, on f. 54v, and his autograph "Querub" on title page). Two notes laid in the manuscript, recording deaths and epitaphs by community members (for example, 1: "Levi Salamone di Giacobbe e di Sacerdotte Enrichetta nato a Vercelli ...").

items.title: Aaron Katz diaries, 1913-1916, Volume 1.
items.creator: Katz, Aaron, 1860-1922
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Modern American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.placeDisplay: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.region: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.type: manuscripts (documents); codices (bound manuscripts); diaries; Manuscripts,  American
items.desc: Comprises four leather-bound, preprinted, pocket calendar diaries published by the Standard Diary Co.  The volumes were kept by Aaron Katz spanning four years from 1913 to 1916.  Katz faithfully wrote daily in his diaries.  He noted the weather each day in one or two words followed by his experiences of the events in his daily life.  Katz noted daily business travels to Poughkeepsie, the Catskills, New York City, and other towns to obtain and sell iron, copper, rails, horseshoes, rags, etc.  One employee Katz mentioned almost daily was Charlie Finn, who he referred to as Finn.  Katz recorded the comings and goings of his sons Albert and Felix including dancing lessons, school, the movies, and attending services at Temple.  He also recorded the daily life of his wife Sophie, shopping, cooking, social gatherings, and friendships.  The Katz's attended movies, plays, and the opera in Kingston.  He recorded social gatherings, dinners, playing cards games, whist, and dominoes with family and friends.  Katz recorded the birthdays of his family and illnesses and deaths of family and friends.  In August each year the Katz family vacationed at Rockaway Park, New York.  In addition to work, family, and friends Katz wrote of his Jewish life. The family sometimes attended Friday evening or Saturday morning services at Temple Emanuel in Kingston a Reform Congregation.  He noted talking with Rabbi Moses Eckstein, going to trustee meetings, attending High Holiday services, and Pesach.  Katz occasionally mentioned national and international news such as Election Day, World War I, and an earthquake in Italy.  A motor vehicle registration card for an E.M.F. Touring car is laid in the 1914 diary.

items.creator: Katz, Aaron, 1860-1922
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Modern American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.placeDisplay: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.region: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.type: manuscripts (documents); codices (bound manuscripts); diaries; Manuscripts,  American
items.desc: Comprises four leather-bound, preprinted, pocket calendar diaries published by the Standard Diary Co.  The volumes were kept by Aaron Katz spanning four years from 1913 to 1916.  Katz faithfully wrote daily in his diaries.  He noted the weather each day in one or two words followed by his experiences of the events in his daily life.  Katz noted daily business travels to Poughkeepsie, the Catskills, New York City, and other towns to obtain and sell iron, copper, rails, horseshoes, rags, etc.  One employee Katz mentioned almost daily was Charlie Finn, who he referred to as Finn.  Katz recorded the comings and goings of his sons Albert and Felix including dancing lessons, school, the movies, and attending services at Temple.  He also recorded the daily life of his wife Sophie, shopping, cooking, social gatherings, and friendships.  The Katz's attended movies, plays, and the opera in Kingston.  He recorded social gatherings, dinners, playing cards games, whist, and dominoes with family and friends.  Katz recorded the birthdays of his family and illnesses and deaths of family and friends.  In August each year the Katz family vacationed at Rockaway Park, New York.  In addition to work, family, and friends Katz wrote of his Jewish life. The family sometimes attended Friday evening or Saturday morning services at Temple Emanuel in Kingston a Reform Congregation.  He noted talking with Rabbi Moses Eckstein, going to trustee meetings, attending High Holiday services, and Pesach.  Katz occasionally mentioned national and international news such as Election Day, World War I, and an earthquake in Italy.  A motor vehicle registration card for an E.M.F. Touring car is laid in the 1914 diary.

items.creator: Katz, Aaron, 1860-1922

items.place: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.placeDisplay: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.region: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.type: manuscripts (documents); codices (bound manuscripts); diaries; Manuscripts,  American
items.desc: Comprises four leather-bound, preprinted, pocket calendar diaries published by the Standard Diary Co.  The volumes were kept by Aaron Katz spanning four years from 1913 to 1916.  Katz faithfully wrote daily in his diaries.  He noted the weather each day in one or two words followed by his experiences of the events in his daily life.  Katz noted daily business travels to Poughkeepsie, the Catskills, New York City, and other towns to obtain and sell iron, copper, rails, horseshoes, rags, etc.  One employee Katz mentioned almost daily was Charlie Finn, who he referred to as Finn.  Katz recorded the comings and goings of his sons Albert and Felix including dancing lessons, school, the movies, and attending services at Temple.  He also recorded the daily life of his wife Sophie, shopping, cooking, social gatherings, and friendships.  The Katz's attended movies, plays, and the opera in Kingston.  He recorded social gatherings, dinners, playing cards games, whist, and dominoes with family and friends.  Katz recorded the birthdays of his family and illnesses and deaths of family and friends.  In August each year the Katz family vacationed at Rockaway Park, New York.  In addition to work, family, and friends Katz wrote of his Jewish life. The family sometimes attended Friday evening or Saturday morning services at Temple Emanuel in Kingston a Reform Congregation.  He noted talking with Rabbi Moses Eckstein, going to trustee meetings, attending High Holiday services, and Pesach.  Katz occasionally mentioned national and international news such as Election Day, World War I, and an earthquake in Italy.  A motor vehicle registration card for an E.M.F. Touring car is laid in the 1914 diary.

items.title: Chassidische Volkslieder
items.creator: Engel, Joel, 1868-1927; Ginsburg, Saul M., 1866-1940; Marek, P. S. (Petr Semenovich), 1862-1920
collections: Gratz-Mandell Jewish Music Collection (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.type: manuscripts (documents); scores (documents for music); Folk music; sheet music
items.desc: A manuscript collection of Yiddish folk songs, almost all copied from Joel Engel's Jüdische Volkslieder, vol. 1 (Moscow: The Author, 191-?, preface dated in 1909). Engel's arrangements are based on songs originally collected by Saul M Ginsburg and Petr Marek, Evrejskija Narodnyja Pěsni V Rossii. Voskhod, 1901. The cover states the name Jüdische Volkslieder and include the initials BK, perhaps the name of the owner or the copyist. The title page however reads Chassidische Volkslieder "after Engel, Ginsburg, and ?". The songs have Yiddish, and at times German and Russian, texts underlay with additional stanzas appearing at the end of some songs without music. The songs were numbered by the cataloguer from 1 to 9. Most songs are for solo with piano accompaniment, except nos. 4 and 6 (for solo without accompaniment) and no. 9, a duet (in Engel's printed work the second voice of this duet is a textless violin part). Titles of the songs are in different languages (Yiddish, German and/or Russian in Latin or Cyrillic characters). The pieces are variously described in the titles as Chassidic, Gypsy-style, soldiers' songs, and love songs. The last four pages are blank, perhaps left to include more songs, as the note "E moll in a" in the upper staff of the last blank page seems to indicate. Another composition for voice and piano by Engel written in a different paper was appended to this manuscript and is numbered no. 9: "Omrim: jeschnah erez." This is an original composition by Joel Engel set to a text by Saul Tchernichowsky. It was published in Shalosh Manginot. = Drei Lieder, Juwal Nr. 122, Gibt's Ein Land: Op. 39, Nr. 1. Berlin and Jerusalem: Juwal, 1923. Although the handwriting does not appear to be Engel's, this manuscript emanates from circles close to the composer around the time of composition and publication, as shown by the date "April 25, 1915" on page 6.

items.title: Sholem Aleichem will and epitaph. 1915
items.creator: Sholem Aleichem, 1859-1916; Miscellaneous Manuscripts Collection (University of Pennsylvania)
collections: Miscellaneous Manuscripts
items.place: Unknown
items.type: manuscripts (documents); poems; wills; Epitaphs; Manuscripts, Yiddish; Manuscripts, American
items.desc: This is a collection of two documents written by Sholem Aleichem, both relating to his death and legacy; he wrote them both as he was nearing the end of his life. As indicated in the text of the will, these two documents were meant to be kept together by the author himself, and the epitaph may have been written at the same time as the will. There are two pieces to the collection; the first being a draft of Sholem Aleichem's will, dated on 11 Tishrei 5676, or (Sunday) 19 September 1915 in New York (262 x 200 mm); the second a draft of his epitaph, undated and without a place of writing (135 x 83 mm). The ethical will contains 33 lines of text, separated by a divider after line 21. The elements in the ethical will are numbered 1 to 5, with (1) the desire to be buried among common folk, (2) the abjuration of all accolades on his tombstone, simply the name Sholem Aleichem and the enclosed Yiddish epitaph, (3) the desire to be remembered through his writings and not with monuments, statues, or other ceremonies, (4) the desire for Kaddish to be recited by his family in his memory, as well as only his cheerful writings, on his yahrzeit (annual anniversary of death), and (5) the preservation of their family's Jewish descent ("Idish upshṭamung") no matter the convictions of his descendants, but the warning to any who join another faith that they forfeit his will and have no place in his family. The financial bequests of the will are numbered 6 through 10. There is a large signature of Sholem ben Menachem Rabinowitz and Sholem Aleichem on the second page of the will. The epitaph is a Yiddish poem written on a card with a dark border in careful stanzas with a signature at the bottom.

items.title: Aaron Katz diaries, 1913-1916, Volume 4.
items.creator: Katz, Aaron, 1860-1922
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Modern American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.placeDisplay: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.region: Kingston (N.Y.) -- Social life and customs -- 20th century
items.type: manuscripts (documents); codices (bound manuscripts); diaries; Manuscripts,  American
items.desc: Comprises four leather-bound, preprinted, pocket calendar diaries published by the Standard Diary Co.  The volumes were kept by Aaron Katz spanning four years from 1913 to 1916.  Katz faithfully wrote daily in his diaries.  He noted the weather each day in one or two words followed by his experiences of the events in his daily life.  Katz noted daily business travels to Poughkeepsie, the Catskills, New York City, and other towns to obtain and sell iron, copper, rails, horseshoes, rags, etc.  One employee Katz mentioned almost daily was Charlie Finn, who he referred to as Finn.  Katz recorded the comings and goings of his sons Albert and Felix including dancing lessons, school, the movies, and attending services at Temple.  He also recorded the daily life of his wife Sophie, shopping, cooking, social gatherings, and friendships.  The Katz's attended movies, plays, and the opera in Kingston.  He recorded social gatherings, dinners, playing cards games, whist, and dominoes with family and friends.  Katz recorded the birthdays of his family and illnesses and deaths of family and friends.  In August each year the Katz family vacationed at Rockaway Park, New York.  In addition to work, family, and friends Katz wrote of his Jewish life. The family sometimes attended Friday evening or Saturday morning services at Temple Emanuel in Kingston a Reform Congregation.  He noted talking with Rabbi Moses Eckstein, going to trustee meetings, attending High Holiday services, and Pesach.  Katz occasionally mentioned national and international news such as Election Day, World War I, and an earthquake in Italy.  A motor vehicle registration card for an E.M.F. Touring car is laid in the 1914 diary.

items.desc: Printed ketubah form with manuscript standard ketubah text in black ink in Aramaic in Sephardic semi-cursive script. Decorative border and columns, crowns above columns, and wood-block engravings of the Western Wall, Rachel's Tomb, and Tomb of Rabbi Meir Baal Haness. Verses from Scripture in block Hebrew print surrounding the ketubah text: abridged verse from Ruth (4:11) and abridged verses from Jeremiah (33:10 and 15:9) at the top; verses from Proverbs 31 (abridged verse 10; verses 29-30) inside left and right borders; verse from Proverbs (18:22) in right column and abridged verse from Ecclesiastes (9:9) in left column. Wedding took place on 25 Elul 5677 (12 Sept. 1917), in Tiberias, Israel. Groom signature between witness signatures, on top of two revenue stamps. Form printed by Defus Sh. Tsuḳerman.

items.title: Pinkas of the Hevra Mishnayot Anshai Sforad Congregation, Roxbury, Massachusetts, 1918-1925; פנקס חברה משניות אנשי ספרד, רקסבורי, מאססאטשוסעטס, 1918-1925
items.creator: Unknown
collections: Arnold and Deanne Kaplan Collection of Modern American Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Massachusetts -- Boston; Roxbury (Boston, Mass.) -- History -- Sources
items.region: Massachusetts -- Boston; Roxbury (Boston, Mass.) -- History -- Sources
items.desc: This is a manuscript of a large ledger created by the Ḥevrat Mishnayot of the Anshei Sforad Congregation of Roxbury Massachusetts, one of the earliest congregations in the United States to follow the Nusaḥ Sefarad rite. The body of the manuscript, including the original bylaws and likely the record of individual group members and leaders, was completed on Monday night, 7 Adar 678 (19 February 1918) in Roxbury, Massachusetts, mentioning the original president, chairmen, and trustees (f. 4r); further bylaws were created on Sunday, 14 Iyyar 681 (22 May 1921, f. 9r); further additions were recorded on Sunday of Parashat ṿa-yetse 686 (December 1, 1925) with a change in chairman and vice-chairman (f. 12r.) The patron of the volume is mentioned as the philanthropist Avraham-Zalman b. Yiśrael Nidel, whose name appears alone on a page surrounded by a decorated shield (f. 3r). The first set of bylaws include the requirement to study the Mishnah with the commentary of R. Ovadiah Bertinoro, to pay a fine of 10 cents per day of neglected study, and to pay annual dues of twenty-five cents. Rewards for the study group include a guaranteed aliyah and returning of the Torah to the ark on the weeks of reading the Ten Commandments (a desirable honor); the inscribing of learning achievements in the pinḳas; study of Mishnayot by the group on behalf of a member who had passed away for the internment period and 30 days since burial (sheloshim), and the further study on the member's yahrzeit; and the honor of a member's wife as a member ("zekhut ke-baʻalah"; in the layout of the manuscript, a member and his complete name and surname are recorded on the verso side, with his wife on the facing recto with only her and her father's Hebrew name; f. 8r-9r). The bylaws of 1921 include the obligation to finish the six orders of the Mishnah twice yearly, on 7 Adar and the first day Seliḥ̣ot are recited, and the neglect of dues will result in the writing of that member having no part in the group in the pinḳas under their name (many names are thus inscribed in the manuscript), and a fine for the calumny of one of the chairpeople (f. 9r, 11r); finally, the 1925 bylaws record the removal of members who ignore appeals for dues, including those who aggressively refuse ("lo hen ṿe-lo śekharan", translated as "not them and not their bounty", taken from Talmud Bavli Berakhot 5b), and the charge of twenty-five dollars to enter the study group (f. 12r). Lettering is stenciled bold black lettering filled in with gold with late Ashkenazic square script below listing yahrzeit or removal from the group.The names continue until f. 255r, with one entry written in 1964 in a cursive hand with a ballpoint pen created to document a yeshiva, not necessarily still in Roxbury, mentioning R. Bernitzky, a visiting rabbinical student from the yeshiva in Lakewood (New Jersey), with the mention of the names of the Rabbis heading the yeshiva: Rabbis Heiman, Rosenson, Wasserman, Kaufer, Trevis, and Mailer, signed by the "steward of the pinḳas" (f. 298r). Folios are heavy varnished paper, with the second free-end featuring a watermark reading "Old Suffolk Mills"; bound in a heavy black leather on board binding with noticeable faux-bands on the spine; also with a red shield in the center of the upper board enclosing the title, likely original.

items.title: Cyrus Adler typescript, Paris Peace Conference, 1919
items.creator: Adler, Cyrus, 1863-1940; Solis-Cohen, D. Hays, -1978; Berger, Elmer, 1908-1996
collections: Penn Digital Collections
items.place: Unknown
items.type: manuscripts (documents); codices (bound manuscripts); correspondence; typescripts; Manuscripts,  American
items.desc: A black, spring-form binder with 395 numbered leaves spanning from March to July 1919.  The volume houses a typescript comprising daily notes, transcriptions of meeting reports, and copies of correspondence documenting Adler's involvement in the Paris Peace Conference as a representative of the American Jewish Committee.  He traveled with Louis Marshall, who was then president of the Jewish Committee.  The typescript appears to be divided into three sections.  The first section, leaves 1 to 73 are Adler's daily entries of his journey to Paris, meetings he attended, diplomatic negotiations, and Jewish relief efforts.  The second section is made up of typescript reports and documents regarding the meetings of Jewish organizations representing Poland, Russia, Galicia, Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia, Turkey, and the Ukraine.  Also represented are Jewish delegations from England and France.  A bill regarding the city of Salonika (Thessaloniki) documents a new plan and rebuilding of the city is also addressed.  One report labeled strictly confidential is titled "Statement of the Zionist Organization regarding Palestine ... proposals to be presented to the Peace Conference."  One of the reports outlines the boundaries for the Jewish state in Palestine.  Recorded are discussions and concerns of atrocities committed against the Jewish people of Poland, Romania, and Ukraine.  There are also reports documenting meetings with President Woodrow Wilson and Herbert Hoover.  Copies of correspondence comprise the third section on leaves 284 to 395.  Diplomats and representatives in the typescript include Julian W. Mack, D. S. Blondheim, Lord Walter Rothschild, Nahum Sokolow and Mary Fels.  Six leaves have been laid in the volume: a three-page letter to D. Hays Solis-Cohen from Elmer Berger dated June 4, 1957, concerning Berger's analysis of the typescript and three leaves of notes regarding the typescript on pink memo paper.

items.desc: Printed, colored ketubah form with standard ketubah text in square letters and manuscript additions in black ink in Aramaic and Hebrew in Sephardic semi-cursive script. Decorative columns, flowers, fruit, wheat, leaves, wreaths and ribbons, and Star of David adorn the text. Verses from Scripture and words of blessing in Hebrew in square letters above the ketubah text. Text of ketubah on right and text of tenaʼim on left; witness signatures appear under each. Groom and bride signatures in Cyrillic under ketubah and groom in Cyrillic under tena'im. Wedding took place on 1 Elul 5684 (31 Aug. 1924), in Filibeh (Plovdiv), Bulgaria. Shemuʼel Papu also signed next to round stamp of the local Jewish community (Rabenu [?] Yiśreʼelit). Three revenue stamps at top right, one at bottom right.

items.creator: Bloch, Joseph Leib, 1860-1930; Hoffmann, Jakob, 1881-1956; Telshe Yeshiva (Telšiai, Lithuania); Jüdische Gemeinde Frankfurt am Main
collections: Rare Judaica Acquisitions Fund
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: Letter of recommendation for Yomtov Lipman Rakow for positions serving as teacher of Hebrew, Rabbinic studies, and Judaics in Germany; Rakow (1884-1950), from Uzda, Belarus (a town southwest of Minsk) taught Hebrew and Rabbinic studies first at the Torah Lehranstalt (headed by Salomon Breuer, who died months before this manuscript in July 1926) and of Jakob Hoffmann, both in Frankfurt; Rakow was to escape Germany at the outbreak of World War II and served as Rosh yeshivah in London (his son, Betzalel Rakow (1927-2003) was a rabbi in Gateshead, England, and head of the Council of Torah Sages, Agudath Israel of Great Britian). Jakob Hoffmann translated (and added to) the letter into German (below Bloch's autograph) and undersigned, dated 24 December 1926. Typed portion in 5 lines; written portion in 9 lines.

items.creator: Unknown
collections: Penn Digital Collections
items.place: Spain -- History -- Civil War, 1936-1939 -- Religious aspects
items.desc: Leaves from a manuscript prayer book, likely comprised of Sephardic prayers not in the printed editions of Siddurim and Mahzorim. The prayers were possibly assembled by a gabbai or cantor, with the communal benediction Berikh shemeh in a Ladino adaptation, a prayer for the traveler, a prayer for a soldier in the military, including combatants in an air force (f. 3r); the manuscript was likely in use in Spain or Portugal and the prayers for Jewish soldiers fighting during the Spanish Civil War. Written in a Sephardic semicursive script, and the final folio written with a ballpoint pen.

collections: Culture Class Collection (University of Pennsylvania)
Bible Culture Class Collection (University of Pennsylvania)
items.place: Unknown
items.desc: Title from preliminary leaf.; Consists of 1 preliminary leaf and 38 individually matted original leaves, with a printed explanatory caption mounted on each mat.; During the years 1938-1950, Ege published portfolios under this title with 37, 50 and 60 leaves.; Includes 37 original leaves from 3 ms. Bibles, 2 printed Bibles from the 15th century, 12 from the 16th, 8 from the 17th century, 4 from the 18th century, 4 from the 19th, and 4 from the 20th century.; Includes 3 ms. leaves on vellum: "Leaf from an Armenian manuscript Bible, 1121 A.D.," "Leaf from a miniature manuscript Bible [Latin Vulgate] circa 1240 A.D.," and "Leaf from a Paris manuscript Bible [Latin Vulgate] circa 1310 A.D."; Each original leaf mounted at left edge in passepartout folder with printed descriptive slip hinged at lower left corner.; Table of contents: Armenian manuscript Bible, 1121 -- Miniature manuscript Bible,  ca 1240 -- Paris manuscript Bible, ca 1310  -- Italian incunabula Bible, 1495 -- Koberger Latin Bible, 1497 -- Aldine Greek Bible, 1518 -- Bible of the Low Countries, 1532 -- Suppressed Luther Bible, 1541 -- Matthew Bible, 1549 -- Great Bible, 1549 -- Giustiniani's Hebrew-Latin Bible, 1551 -- Stephanus Latin Bible, 1555 -- Plantin Louvain Bible, 1565 -- Stephanus Greek New Testament, 1569 -- Bishops' Bible, 1575 -- Genevan, or Breeches Bible, 1592 -- Hamburg Polyglot, 1596 -- Fulke's New Testament, 1601 -- Second printed Spanish Bible, 1602 -- King James Bible, 1611 (2 leaves) -- Pearl Bible, 1653 -- London Polyglot Bible, O.T., 1655 -- London Polyglot Bible, N.T., 1657 -- Elzevir States general Bible, 1663 -- Eliot Indian Bible, 1685 -- Baskett Bible, 1740 -- Germantown Bible, 1763 -- Baskerville Cambridge Bible, 1763 -- Baskerville Birmingham Bible, 1769 -- Thomas Greek New Testament, 1800 -- Thomson's Bible, 1808 -- The Immaculate Bible, 1811 -- Polychrome Bible, 1899 -- Doves Bible, 1903-1905 -- Miniature Bible, 1919 -- Nonesuch Bible, 1924-1925 -- Rogers Oxford Lectern Bible, 1935.; Culture Class Collection copy has, included in same portfolio, an additional 6 leaves with bookseller's (Dawson's Book Shop) descriptions. Kelmscott Press, leaf from Sidonia the Sorceress printed by William Morris in 1893 -- The Ibarra Sallust, leaf from edition of Sallust printed at Madrid by Joachin Ibarra, 1772 -- Manuscript on vellum, Armenian Bible leaf written on animal skin, fifteenth century -- Nuremburg Chronicle leaf, printed from moveable type by Anton Koberger in 1493, first edition -- Chinese block printing, leaf from Buddhist Scriptures printed from wooden blocks in 1440 A.D. -- Leaf from the first collected edition of Chaucer, made by William Thyne, in 1532, printed in London by Thomas Godfray.

items.title: Letter to aunt in Palestine, November 14, 1937. = בריעוו צו טענטע אין פאלעסטינע, דעם 14 צו נאוועמבער 1937.
items.creator: Hindeh, (Sokoliki Górskie, Poland); Abraham J. and Deborah Karp Collection of Judaica (University of Pennsylvania)
collections: Penn Digital Collections
items.place: Poland; Israel; Lutowiska (Poland) -- 20th century -- Correspondence; Israel
items.type: manuscripts (documents); personal correspondence; correspondence artifacts; autographs (manuscripts)
items.desc: This is a letter written from Hindeh, a woman living in Sokoliki Górskie, Poland (a village in the far south east Poland, immediately west of the Ukranian border) writing expansively to inform her aunt in Palestine of family news. The letter covers various weddings, news about children in the family, the family business, and questions about life in Palestine; a postscript asks about something written about Palestine in the newspaper. Sokoliki Górskie had a very small Jewish community and was apparently sheltered from the recent developments of the eastward expansions of the Nazi regime. Written on both sides; written in a Yiddish cursive script.
subjects: Manuscripts, Yiddish -- Poland -- Sokoliki -- 20th century -- Specimens

items.desc: Title devised by cataloger.; Musical directions in Italian and English, mostly abbreviated; Hebrew titles and text are vary between both romanized Hebrew and Hebrew script.; The collection includes a selection of works presented in both original and arranged versions. Several pieces appear multiple times, each in a distinct arrangement for different instruments. The materials consist of individually numbered creative works; however, the numbering is inconsistent, with items appearing out of order and some numbers duplicated or missing. A number of works lack formal titles, and others are incomplete, containing no lyrics or substantive content beyond their numbering. Taken together, the materials appear to represent drafts, working copies, or partial versions rather than finalized compositions.; Table of contents: Ṿe-shamru / A. No inventory is currently available for this collection. Please contact SCRC by emailing scrc@temple.edu or by calling 215-204-8257 to request additional information about this collection. When submitting your request, please provide collection ID and title.

Copies of the Friday Forum column written by Glaser for The Jewish Exponent, 1975-1976; two copies of a typed manuscript "Tides of Time" or "A Story of the Holocaust;" manuscript copies of "letters to the editor" and accompanying published version that appeared in the newspaper primarily submitted to The Jewish Exponent and the Philadelphia Evening Bulletin; sheet music with lyrics and music by Glaser; the bulk of the collection consists of manuscript articles, essays, poems, and plays, 1968-1974 written by Glaser in both English and Yiddish, including some translations from Yiddish to English of works written by others.

items.collection: Harvey Finkle photographs
items.title: Jewish Holocaust Survivors, prints (volume 1 of 2)
items.creator: Finkle, Harvey
collections: Harvey Finkle photographs
items.place: Philadelphia (Pa.)
items.desc: Black-and-white photographic prints which, according to Finkle's notes, is "an attempt to document how Survivors put their lives together after suffering from the horrors of the Holocaust." Prints feature portraits and candid photographs of families, food stores, a garment factory, a gathering at the statue of what is now the Horowitz-Wasserman Holocaust Memorial Plaza, home life, playing music, news articles, old family pictures, schools, tailor shops, and graphic historic images of the Holocaust. Images include Miriam Levinson (p. 1-30); Nina Kaleska (p. 31-54); Bernard Mednicki (p. 55-108); Joe and Ruby Zbik Tailers at 7th and South (p. 109-136); Clara Isaacman whose husband was head of Jewish College (p. 137-156); Ilse and Leo Korona (p. 157-180); Kupferberg family (p. 181-196); and an unidentified woman who inherited Stenton Cleaners (p. 197-214). Harvey Finkle (born March 28, 1934) is a self-taught documentary still photographer and photojournalist who has documented social, economic, cultural, and political issues across the city of Philadelphia, the United States, and the world. Finkle's work largely focuses on activism relating to historically underrepresented communities, including people living on low income, unhoused/unsheltered/houseless people/people experiencing homelessness, refugees, immigrants, and disabled people.

Andy Mager; Andrew L. Mager; born 1961; indicted in 1984 for refusing to register for the US military draft and was sentenced to six months in prison plus two years of probation; served time in prison for protesting cruise missile deployment at Griffiss Air Force Base; active in movements for peace, social justice and environmental protection as an organizer, trainer, activist, writer and speaker; worked with people at the Onondaga Nation and was a cofounder of Neighbors of the Onondaga Nation; worked as an organizer for the Syracuse Peace Council, 2002-2012; has written about and been interviewed on his stance as a Jewish conscientious objector.

Jehoshua A. Gilboa was born in Pinsk, Poland, as Yeshoshua A. Globerman, on May 13, 1918. During World War II he was imprisoned in Russian prisons and camps. Following the war, he married Dina Firstenberg in 1948 and moved to Israel in 1949. He completed his Masters Degree in 1967 at Boston University and his Doctorate at Tel Aviv University in 1975. His doctoral thesis was on Hebrew culture in the Soviet Union.

Much of Gilboa's professional life was spent as a journalist. He worked for several daily newspapers in Tel Aviv: as a member of the editorial board of the Dvar (1950-1953), as assistant editor and editor-in-chief at the Zmanim (1953-1955), and at the Maariv as a member of the editorial staff beginning in 1955. He worked at the Institute of East European Studies at Brandeis University as a senior research associate (1965-1967) and was a research associate at Tel Aviv University's Diaspora Research Institute (beginning in 1969). From 1973-1978 he served as editor of the scholarly journal Shvut , which sought to preserve the heritage of Russian Jewry. During the 1960s, he also contributed a number of articles to The Jerusalem Post .

In addition, he wrote or edited a number of books, including "Confess! Eight Years in Soviet Prisons" (1968), "The Black Years of Soviet Jewry 1939-1953" (1971), "The Kibbutz Sitting Pretty" (1973), and "A Language Silenced: The Suppression of Hebrew Literature and Culture in the Soviet Union" (1982). He was also an editor and contributor to several anthologies of short stories and essays in Hebrew and Yiddish. In addition to Hebrew, Yiddish and English, Gilboa had some knowledge of Polish, Russian, and German. He was awarded the Israeli Journalist Prize in 1965 and 1971 and won the Prize of Judaistic Studies in 1972.

Gilboa died in 1981 following a brief illness. He was survived by his wife and two children.

(This biography was written using an obituary from The Jerusalem Post (February 5, 1981) and an entry on Gilboa from Contemporary Authors Online (Gale, 2007).

items.title: Middle East: Israel, prints
items.creator: Finkle, Harvey
collections: Harvey Finkle photographs
items.place: Middle East; Jerusalem; Tel Aviv (Israel)
items.desc: Black-and-white photographic prints depicting daily life in Israel, featuring ceremonies, Christian processions, food establishments, health clinics, homeless/houseless/unhoused/unsheltered shelters, recreation centers, Romanian workers (p. 195-202), synagogues, and the Western Wall. Harvey Finkle (born March 28, 1934) is a self-taught documentary still photographer and photojournalist who has documented social, economic, cultural, and political issues across the city of Philadelphia, the United States, and the world. Finkle's work largely focuses on activism relating to historically underrepresented communities, including people living on low income, unhoused/unsheltered/houseless people/people experiencing homelessness, refugees, immigrants, and disabled people.

items.desc: Photographer's note: Tu B'Schvat; Hayda Pasha synagogue. Grand Rabbin David Asseo comes to visit. Tu B’Shvat was actually a day to calculate the age of various trees for the sole purpose of tithing. in accordance to biblical scriptures it is stated that fruit may not be taken from a tree in the tree's first three years of life. The fourth year fruit harvest was offered as a burnt offering to God. On the fifth year of the tree the fruit could be eaten. The schvat was considered to be a tree's birthday, since it was believed that trees had aged by one year on this day. This actually takes place on the 15th of Shvat. Shvat is the month that typically falls between January to February. The name Shevat or in Hebrew; Shevat is mentioned in biblical scripture and as adopted during the exile of the Babylonian Jewish people. It is now considered the New Year For trees. Today, on Tu B' Shvat for kids, children plant trees or even donare money for trees to be planted.

items.desc: Photographer's note: The main reading desk, or teva (Ashkenazi: bima) of the Ahrida synagogue of Balat is shaped like a ship at sea with its prow pointing towards the Ark. The significance of this shape is uncertain. Simon Tov, the synagogue's caretaker, suggests that it was intended to represent Noah's ark, which some believe came to rest on Mt. Ararat in eastern Turkey. Others consider the teva’s form a memorial to the ships which brought the Spanish Jews to the Ottoman Empire in 1492.

items.desc: Photographer's note: I asked Izzet Bana, a noted singer of Sephardic songs and a teacher, to identify the people in this photograph taken on Büyükada Island in 1985. His response in Ladino was: “Ya topi ken son. La kaza ya ez derokada en Büyükada-kumsal. El hombre ke esta asentado: Varujan Bey – (Barış Kuyumculuğun Sahibi)10 anyos antes sero labotika i agora bive en Kanada los otros/as no son konosidos/as.” Translation: “Now I know who they are: The house where they are sitting has been torn down. The man seated in front is Varujan Bey. Ten years before he closed his store and now lives in Canada. I don’t know who the other people are”.

items.desc: Photographer's note: Turkey is still a country where people have time for the simple pleasures of life, and one of them is card playing. On any given Sunday afternoon at the Horozlu Casino of Büyükada there is always a friendly game of Relans or Konken underway. The ladies like to entertain each other every now and then with a song in Judæo/Spanish. (They also asked me to mention that not all Turkish Jewish ladies play cards!)

items.desc: Photographer's note: Each year for the holiday of Sukkoth, Simon Tov the ªhammaªh or caretaker of the Yanbol and Ahrida synagogues, makes bouquets of leaves from the bushes found in the synagogues’ courtyards. This bouquet, or arava (Hebrew: ‘willow’) is used in a ritual during the morning services of the seventh day of Sukkoth, where it may symbolize life’s continuity. Later, the arava is taken home and hung at the entrance of the house to ensure a productive year.

items.desc: Photographer's note: The Galata Tower, one of the most prominent landmarks on the left bank of the Golden Horn, was built by the Genoese in the 14th century. It is at the center of a district called Kuledibi, meaning “at the foot of the tower.” By the turn of the century, large numbers of Jews were moving here and to nearby Pera (now called Beyoµlu). The new address implied a higher social status, as this was then the area for Europeans and the well-to-do. Here the community built schools and the offices of the Chief Rabbinate, as well as synagogues. (Note on the map of Istanbul that this area shows the highest concentration of synagogues.) This area along with Balat and Hasköy, was mainly Jewish until the 1950's when many of Istanbul's Jews moved on to Israel.

items.desc: Photographer's note: Ahrida synagogue at Purim. It is one of Istanbul’s oldest synagogues, built by Romaniotes (Greek Jews) 550 years ago, and located in the Balat neighborhood. I remember Turkey’s then Chief Rabbi David Asseo giving a sermon in Ladino there in which he admonished those present not to marry out of the faith. At the time, few did it. Today marrying out of the faith is more common.

items.desc: Photographer's note: The Ortaköy cemetery on the European shore of the Bosphorus commands a wonderful view of the Atatürk Bridge which links Europe with Asia. Ortaköy was once home to João Miguez, the Portuguese converso better known as the Duke of Naxos. He was a well-respected advisor to two sultans and benefactor of his co-religionists in the Ottoman Empire and elsewhere. He was granted title to the lands around Lake Tiberias where he hoped to establish a Jewish Colony. One of the larger contracting firms, Alarko, owned by Jewish builders I.shak Alaton and Üzeyir Garih, is currently building luxurious town houses in the hills surrounding the old Jewish Cemetery of Ortaköy.

collections: Laurence and Ayşe Gürsan-Salzmann Collection
items.place: Turkey -- Büyükada
items.desc: Photographer's note: Turkey is a country where people have time for board games and cards. Generally among the Jews, women are the card players, and men the board players. The most popular game is TAVLA or Şeş Beş. It is the Persian name for the game that is commonly called backgammon. It is played at home, but more often than not, in a public space like a cafe or, as it is shown here, on Büyükada Island. During the years we lived in Turkey I had time to perfect my backgammon skills, and learn to call out the numbers on the dice in Persian, the country where this game is said to have originated. (Şeş beş is six and five, a desired dice throw with which to begin the game). Summers on Büyükada and the other nearby Princess Islands provided Turkey's Jews with the most idlyic of places to enjoy past times and be with family. Their were clubs to accommodate all sizes of pocket books and of course always a friendly game of Tavla, backgammon with one's friends. Büyükada now in summer is frequented by wealthy and not so wealthy Arabs escaping the heat of the desert and enjoy the pleasures of the Princess Islands that Turkey's Jews have long enjoyed. So, Arabic has now replaced the Ladino, French and Greek that used to be commonly heard.

items.desc: Photographer's note: Gabai Eskenasi Kapparot: a custom in which the sins of a person are symbolically transferred to a fowl held above a person's head shortly before Yom Kippur. It is practiced by some Jews in Istanbul who shortly before Yom Kippur visit Gabai Eskenasi who swings a chicken above the person's head in a circle three times while reciting a prayer that says: "This is my exchange, my substitute, my atonement; this rooster (or hen) shall go to its death, but I shall go to a good, long life, and to peace." The hope is that the fowl, which is then donated to the poor for food, will take on any misfortune that might otherwise occur to the one who has taken the ritual, in punishment for his or her sins.

Jannine Miller at voting station at 16th and Ridge St., North Philadelphia (p. 253-254, 285-286, 289-290, 341-342, 247-248, 349-350); Sam Santiago, outreach worker (p. 271-272, 327-328); Residents of St. Columba (p. 281-288, 339-340); and voting station at 16th and Ridge St., North Philadelphia (p. 341-342, 347-350). Harvey Finkle (born March 28, 1934) is a self-taught documentary still photographer and photojournalist who has documented social, economic, cultural, and political issues across the city of Philadelphia, the United States, and the world. Finkle's work largely focuses on activism relating to historically underrepresented communities, including people living on low income, unhoused/unsheltered/houseless people/people experiencing homelessness, refugees, immigrants, and disabled people.
